overview: This record covers the First World War transition from German Togoland to British and French occupation. German colonial forces surrendered in August 1914; the territory was divided in 1916. The imported 1914 to 1920 window is not the lifetime of modern independent Togo. People across this colonial territory spoke different languages and maintained communities extending beyond its changing borders.

periods.title: War and occupation
periods.summary: British and French forces took over after the German surrender.

periods.title: Partition before the mandates
periods.summary: Separate occupation zones preceded the League of Nations arrangements.

periods.title: Formal mandates
periods.summary: The League’s documents defined British and French responsibilities and a dividing border.

items.text: Conquest brought years of administrative work. The National Archives has catalogued records from 1914 to 1926 concerning occupied Togoland and Cameroon, including the handling of seized German property. The archive connects military victory with the practical questions that followed: who would govern, and what would happen to colonial assets?

At Kamina near Atakpamé, a radio station linked the colony with Nauen near Berlin by April 1914. Its nine steel antenna structures were accompanied by steam-powered machinery, wells, pumps and water treatment. Sending a message across continents required much more than an operator tapping a key.

Building Kamina involved a temporary seven-kilometre railway for materials, a brickworks and a carpentry workshop. The German colonial administration supplied about 100 forced workers from northern Togo; people from around Atakpamé, especially Akposso workers, were also recruited. A spectacular machine rested on hard, unequally paid human labor.

German operators destroyed Kamina’s radio station during the night of 24 to 25 August 1914 as British and French forces approached. Ruins preserve the remains of a technology whose strategic usefulness made it a target almost as soon as it entered service.

An Ewe cotton cloth dated around 1900 to 1920 survives as a gown in the British Museum. Its extra decorative weft threads show the weaver’s pattern-making skill. Curators think a later tailor converted an originally rectangular formal cloth into the gown: an object can have more than one wardrobe life.

A fibre-and-leather apron collected in colonial Togoland before its 1919 museum donation offers a very different clothing example. The register identifies its makers as Frafra, grouped by the museum under Grusi. The broad colonial place-name does not tell us the exact village; this was one local tradition among many.

Mission schools in the Ewe-speaking region taught reading, writing, physical exercises and Bible lessons. Ewe became a language of teaching and church life, while colonial policies later promoted German. Schooling could open access to written knowledge while also pressuring children to adopt the religion and cultural priorities of European missions.

A later photograph, probably taken between 1933 and 1937, shows a mission-school class in two rows, wearing uniforms, outside a building with classrooms and a planted terrace. The children appear barefoot. This carefully dated glimpse of school life comes after the map window, under the colonial order that followed partition.

Westermann’s 1905 Ewe dictionary describes amla as a bush knife also used as a hoe, manufactured especially in Akpafu. One tool could help with more than one farming job. Such a small dictionary entry preserves evidence of local craft production and useful equipment alongside the much louder story of colonial machines.

Written language sample: “Akpafumla” means “bush knife from Akpafu.” The word appears in Westermann’s 1905 Ewe dictionary under amla, and later linguist Mark Dingemanse gives this English gloss. This Latin-script Ewe word records the association between a useful product and the place that made it.

In September 1919, a petition signed by chiefs objected that placing Togo under France would separate Ewe-speaking people from relatives and communities in the southeastern Gold Coast and hamper economic progress. Their argument reminds us that a border drawn by colonial powers could interrupt an existing social and trading world.

The 1922 French mandate survives as a document in French and English. Its twelve articles defined the territory and duties including suppressing slave trading, protecting religious freedom and respecting local laws and customs. These were promises in a governing document; the manuscript itself cannot show how faithfully they were carried out.

ending.text: German rule ended in 1914, but colonial rule continued under Britain and France. The 1922 mandates formalized a divided territory; the map’s 1920 endpoint is not independence. Communities, languages, crafts and demands for political change continued across the new boundary.
